---AGENTS---
# Writing style — comments, help text, and CLI output

This file is the house style for everything a reader sees: Go doc comments,
`--help` output, and the strings a command prints or returns as errors. It
applies to every Go file in this repository. Keep it short enough that it can
be re-read before every PR.

---

## Code comments

**Explain why, not what changed.** A comment answers the question the code
cannot: the invariant, the trade-off, the reason a non-obvious choice is the
safe one. It never narrates history.

- Never reference a PR, issue, fix, or the past tense of the code itself.
  "Used to", "now", "previously", "after the refactor", "fixes #123" are all
  forbidden. Git history already knows; the reader of the code does not care.
- A doc comment on every exported symbol. One or two sentences is usually
  enough. `golint` enforces this; don't make a reviewer do it.
- Target ≤ 10 lines per doc block. If you need more, the extra content
  belongs in `docs/` or a README, not above the function.
- "Deliberately not X" comments are encouraged when they stop a plausible
  wrong refactor. `internal/gitops/remote.go` is the exemplar: it says the
  function is *not* used to derive the cache directory, and why.
- No TODO, FIXME, HACK, or XXX in committed code. File an issue instead.

---

## Help text (cobra)

`--help` is reference material, not a blog post. A reader in a terminal wants
to know what the command does, what it costs, and which flags change the
behavior. Philosophy and motivation belong in `docs/`.

- **`Short:`** one line, imperative verb, no trailing period.
  Good: `Pin a component's image digest into an environment`
  Bad:  `This command pins the image digest.`
- **`Long:`** target ≤ 150 words, hard ceiling ~200. Cover: what it does,
  what it reads, what it writes, what can go wrong that the user can prevent.
  Cut: why the command exists, why GitOps is good, architecture essays.
- **`Use:`** positional args in `<>`, optional in `[]`, variadic as `name...`.
  Good: `pin <component> [version]`
  Bad:  `pin COMPONENT [VERSION]`, `pin <component> [<version>]`

If a `Long:` draft exceeds 200 words, the excess is almost always the second
paragraph onwards. Move it to a file under `docs/` and keep the help text
to usage.

---

## Flag descriptions

Use the shared constants in `cmd/intropy/flagtext.go`. Never hand-write a new
description for a flag another command already has:

- `--output`, `--env`, `--gitops-repo`, `--argocd-server`, `--domain`,
  `--system`, `--template-version` all have constants.
- If you add a flag that several commands will share, add a constant first.
- Flag descriptions are fragments, not sentences: no trailing period, no
  "This flag…". Start with the noun. Good: `target environment (required)`.

---

## Runtime output

A CLI's output is read twice: once by a human scanning, once by a script
parsing. The two never share a stream.

- **stdout is for results.** Tables, JSON, the thing the command was run to
  produce.
- **stderr is for everything else.** Progress, warnings, completion messages,
  errors. A pipeline reading stdout must never see a status line.

### Voice

- Progress and completion: **lowercase, present tense, no trailing period**.
  Good: `syncing api on argocd.example.com at a1b2c3d`
  Good: `published ghcr.io/example/releases/api:1.2.0`
  Bad:  `Published ghcr.io/…`  `Sync complete.`
- Empty states follow the same rule: `no releases found`, not
  `No releases found.`
- A follow-up hint naming a command goes on its own line, in backticks:
  `use 'intropy release create <component>' to publish one`

### Errors

- Front-load what failed. The remediation, if there is one, goes on a second
  line. Do not editorialize — the user is already reading an error.
  Good: `pending change is a1b2c3d, not the f4e5d6c you reviewed`
        `run 'intropy deploy diff api --env staging' before syncing`
  Bad:  `…has advanced since you reviewed it — you really should read the new diff…`
- Wrap errors with context as they travel up: `fmt.Errorf("pull %s: %w", …)`.
  The outermost prefix names the command or operation, not the internals.

### Vocabulary

- **image digest**, not "bits", "artifacts", or "the images".
- **environment** in prose, `--env` only when naming the flag.
- A template's message **direction** is derived from its block kind: an
  extractor publishes, a loader subscribes, a transactional integration
  wires no messages. The flags follow it: `--publishes` for producing
  templates, `--subscribe` for consuming templates.
- **message** is a message definition: a registry entry (`message list`,
  `message show <ref>`) or a producing component's `publishes` declaration.
  A subscription is written to the record as a `subscribe` block; a
  producer's as `publishes`. **event** is prose for the runtime occurrence
  of a message, never a scaffold value. `contract` survives only where the
  .NET shared-project type name is literally meant — transitional.
- `->` for a transition (`1.0 -> 1.1`), ` @ ` for a pin (`api @ 1.2.0`).
  Never mix the two in one message.
- A commit SHA is shown short (7 chars) unless the full value is the point.

### Command verbs

One verb per meaning, used on every noun (`int`, `template`, `deploy`, ...).
The full set, grouped by what the verb does to the world:

**Read-only** — exit 0 even when the answer is "they disagree", never write
to git, never trigger a sync:

- **`list`** enumerates a collection: integrations on disk, templates in the
  library, published releases. It never prints one item's
  details.
- **`show`** prints the details of exactly one thing: a template's manifest,
  an integration's scaffold record. It never enumerates.
- **`status`** reports one component across every environment, one row
  each, and whether the rows agree. It never prints one environment's
  details — that is `show`.
- **`diff`** prints the rendered change a `sync` would apply, as the
  resources themselves. Both sides are committed revisions; it never diffs
  an uncommitted worktree.
- **`inspect`** prints the deployment model derived from one system topology:
  components, workloads, ports, and available local fixtures. It never
  renders manifests or writes project or Git state.
- **`render`** emits a complete Kubernetes YAML stream for one environment.
  It may ask for missing local fixture choices, buffers and validates the whole
  stream before writing stdout, writes all interaction and diagnostics to
  stderr, and never changes project, Git, or cluster state.

**Create or change project state** — may write files under the project.
Manifest creation may push a review branch, never the default branch:

- **`create`** makes something new from a template or from scaffolded
  parts: an integration, a system host, a release manifest to publish, or
  missing Kubernetes manifests on a GitOps review branch. Manifest creation
  accepts existing identical files but never replaces or deletes a file.
- **`add`** attaches something that already exists elsewhere to this
  project: a library registration. Unlike
  `create`, the content is pulled, not generated.

  `create`, the content is pulled, not generated.
- **`update`** reconciles something installed against the ref its source
  now pins: a cached index against the registry. It never changes which
  ref is pinned — that is the publisher's job.
**Move or publish** — change what runs somewhere or what others can pull:

- **`publish`** pushes an immutable artifact to an OCI registry: a release
  manifest. What is published cannot be edited in
  place; a new version is a new publish.
- **`pin`** writes one component's image digest into one environment's
  overlay.
- **`promote`** copies the digests one environment runs into the next
  environment in the promotion graph.
- **`sync`** applies an environment's pending change through ArgoCD. It
  never decides what the change is — that is `pin` and `promote`.
- **`use`** selects which named customer context subsequent commands act
  on. Neither `update` (reconciles an installed thing against its source)
  nor `pin` (writes one component's digest) covers selecting the operator's
  active context, and `use` is the name kubeconfig muscle memory expects
  for it. It never creates or edits contexts — those are authored in the
  config file by hand.

Do not import kubectl's `get`/`describe` split — `int describe` was retired
because it described templates, not integrations. New verbs need a reason
that the set above cannot express, and the reason goes in this file with
the verb, not in a commit message.

---

## What this file is not

It does not replace `CONTRIBUTING.md` (workflow, tests, commit convention) or
`README.md` (what the CLI is). When those disagree with this file, this file
wins on writing style and loses on everything else.

- **Verb-awareness at the CLI layer.** The `xregistry` package's error
  types stay neutral data carriers; `cmd/intropy` wraps
  `NoProducerError` with the publish remediation ("register the producing
  endpoint in the registry first") and rewords the ambiguity listing (R3).
- **Direction gate tolerates absent `block-kind`.** A kind-less
  message-capable template keeps today's behavior for either flag; the
  gate rejects only known-mismatched kinds (extractor + `--subscribe`,
  loader + `--publishes`) and known no-messaging kinds
  (transactional-integration + either flag). AE2's hello-world case fails
  earlier on the message-parameters gate, unchanged.
- **The gate becomes symmetric.** `--subscribe` against an extractor
  template gains the mirror-image usage error. This is a deliberate
  tightening implied by R6/R7's direction model — a CLI that knows
  direction cannot let either flag vanish silently.
- **`contract` stays a template parameter.** The registry has no
  contract concept; `--publishes` seeds only the message parameter, and
  contract is prompted/defaulted/`--set` as today (resolves origin
  deferred question 2).
- **No pick-list pre-filtering.** The prompt offers the same candidate
  pool as subscribe (registry refs + workspace messages); resolution
  errors surface on selection with remediation (resolves origin deferred
  question 1).
- **CLI-written block wins.** When `--publishes` writes
  `SetValues[KeyPublishes]`, it takes precedence over any
  template-derived publishes block for the same run — the snapshot is the
  authoritative wiring.

---

## Open Questions

### Resolved During Planning

- Pick-list pre-filtering (origin, deferred): no pre-filter; resolution
  errors on selection, mirroring subscribe's flow.
- `contract` population under `--publishes` (origin, deferred): remains a
  template parameter; resolution does not touch it.
- Verb-aware error wording (origin, deferred): wrap at the CLI layer;
  `internal/xregistry/errors.go` texts stay neutral.

### Deferred to Implementation

- Exact wording of the publish-side remediation lines: follows the house
  style (front-load the failure, remediation on the second line), tuned
  against the existing subscribe errors.
- How precedence over a template-derived publishes block is enforced
  (SetValues ordering vs explicit removal): visible once the extractor
  template's derived-values shape is in front of the implementer.

---

## Implementation Units

- [x] U1. **Publish-block shape and direction vocabulary**

**Goal:** Extend the wiring vocabulary so a publishes block can carry a
full channel snapshot, and give direction a single CLI-owned home.

**Requirements:** R4, R5, R6

**Dependencies:** None

## Scope Boundaries

- No CLI changes (except the optional T4 guard noted under Open Questions —
  deliberately deferred to a CLI follow-up).
- No changes to deploy-component, deploy-host, shared-contracts, or the
  transactional template (transactional-integration wires no messages).
- No codegen of types from `dataschema` (an external tool's job, per the
  subscribe doc's A2) — the producer only records the pin.
- No changes to CloudEvent identity *defaults* for the flag-less flow.

---

## Context & Research (verified on template-repo main, ac434c3, tag v0.9.0)

- `extractor/template.yaml` — required `topic` + `contract`; labeled
  extractor/in; `values:` derives `eventTypeValue` from topic (`<org>.
  <first>.<last>`), `pubsub: 'pubsub'` hardcoded; **no** derived publish
  block.
- `loader/template.yaml` — same shape; `SubscriptionRoute = "/events/{{ .topic }}"`.
- `extractor/skeleton/src/Constants.cs.tmpl` — renders `PubSubName` ("pubsub"
  literal), `TopicName` = `{{ .topic }}`, `EventSource`/`EventType` with the
  override-else-derive pattern already in place.
- `loader/skeleton/src/Constants.cs.tmpl` — same pattern + `SubscriptionRoute`.
- `system-host/template.yaml` — payload parameters: name, topics, ports,
  components, sharedContracts. **No `messages`.**
- `system-host/skeleton/Topics.cs.tmpl` — ranges `.topics`, derives field
  names, renders `TopicRef<T>`; collisions fail the render loudly.
- `system-host/skeleton/Program.cs` — `graph` verb delegates to
  `IntropyGenerate.Run(assembly, args)` from **Intropy.Topology.Generation**;
  there is no messagegroup code anywhere in the skeleton, and no `MessageGroup`
  in the intropy-topology model (only Topics materialized from edges).
- CLI-side: `internal/system/assemble.go` aggregates internal publishes into
  `Model.Messages`; `payload.go` writes `{name, type, contract?, dataschema?,
  publisher?}`; `update.go` matches that shape; external publishes are
  excluded from both.

---

## Key Technical Decisions

- **One optional `message` parameter, not a rename of anything.** The
  message id is a distinct fact (CloudEvents type) from the topic; a new
  optional parameter plus a precedence rule is additive and keeps the
  flag-less flow byte-identical. Required-ness stays off the flag path:
  required parameters would force both the flag and a prompt.
- **Snapshot-first rendering precedence.** The block is the CLI-owned truth
  for channel and message; params remain the authoring surface for
  out-of-registry flows. `topic` becomes optional: present → prompted
  internal flow as today; absent with a block → block wins; absent with
  `message` (internal) → the CLI's convention (topic = message name) renders
  into Constants so a topic-less producer still builds a coherent record and
  render without the CLI changing.
- **The derived-block guard is a template-repo discipline, not code.** No
  template derives `subscribe`/`publishes` in `spec.values` (none does
  today); a CLI-side hard guard stays deferred (see Open Questions).
- **Messagegroups render from the payload `messages` inside the host, behind
  a clean seam.** The host skeleton renders the message registry from the
  `messages` payload; where the graph section is composed — Generation vs a
  host-side wrapper — is the fork under Open Questions, resolved during
  implementation by reading IntropyGenerate's discovery contract.
- **Versioning: `v0.10.0-rc.1`** before stable. Additive shapes, old records
  read unchanged; rc keeps CI current while the CLI pins settle.

---

## Open Questions

### Resolved During Planning

- Pan-template scope: only loader, extractor, system-host touch messaging.
  streaming-extractor/apiservice exist only on other branches — out of scope
  here, but T1's pattern applies when they land.
- The event-identity override parameters (`eventType`, `eventSource`) keep
  their slot in the precedence chain — they are the migration escape hatches
  the CLI resolution sits above, not competitors.

### Deferred to Implementation

- **T3 seam (Needs research):** where the topology `messagegroups` section is
  composed. Candidate (a) — extend Intropy.Topology's model + Generation
  composition, if discovery can see the rendered message registry; candidate
  (b) — the host's graph wrapper injects the section into the JSON it prints.
  Decide by reading `IntropyGenerate.Run`'s discovery contract; (b) is the
  smaller change but keeps the section out of the model that owns topology
  shape.
- **Injector shape:** what the skeleton's message registry artifact looks
  like (static class of typed message definitions vs data file) — decide
  against how Generation discovers inputs.
- Prompt UX for the optional `message` parameter on the no-flag path (offer?
  omit? registry pick list fires only when the parameter is required-pending
  — verify against CLI prompting, which works for any declared message
  parameter).

---

10	// Version's attributes are NOT repeated on the Resource. For messages —

13	// multi-version resources whose versions each carry isdefault.

16	// collections are top-level group collections; an absent collection decodes
17	// as an empty map, so a caller never nil-checks.

20	# Purpose
21	
22	<!-- One paragraph: wiring values the registry already owns (CloudEvents type,
23	pubsub, topic, schema) were typed by hand into template prompts; internal
24	events used a different vocabulary than cross-system events. One formal
25	vocabulary — message — replaces both. -->
26	
27	# Concepts
28	
29	| Concept | Meaning |
30	| --- | --- |
31	| Message | A message definition. Comes from the read-only xRegistry (external) or a producing component's `publishes` block (internal). |
32	| Subscribe | Written into a component's record as a `subscribe` block. An internal block names only the message; assembly resolves its channel from the producer. An external block carries the full snapshot (pubsub, topic, dataschema, pinned schema version URL). |
33	| Publishes | A producer's declaration: `message` (doubles as the CloudEvents type) plus the transitional `contract` (the .NET shared-project type name). |
34	| Channel | `<pubsub>/<topic>` — producer-declared on the registry, resolved from the publisher in assembly for internal subscriptions. |
35	| Counterparty | Who is on the other end of an external declaration. A `subscribe` block records `producer` (the registry endpoint that publishes the message, in another system) and `group` (the message's registry group); a `publishes` block records `group` only, since its producer is the component itself. Both are snapshots taken at resolution: the flow view draws the producing endpoint outside the system boundary from them, and nothing re-asks the registry. |
36	
37	# Invariants
38	
39	- `sys create`/`sys update` never contact the registry; external
40	  subscriptions carry their own snapshot.
41	- Records written today use the block shape only. Legacy flat
42	  `topic`/`contract`/`pubsub` records stay functional and read as
43	  `publishes`/`subscribe` derived from the block kind (extractor publishes,
44	  loader subscribes).
45	- An internal subscription whose message no component publishes is an
46	  assembly error, not a rendered half-wired system.
47	- `dataschemaurl` pins the schema's default version at subscribe time;
48	  re-pinning is a future re-resolve flow.
49	- A producing workspace records nothing about who subscribes: consumer
50	  endpoints live only in the registry. Both directions are therefore
51	  visible, but not equally: a consuming system's producer comes from the
52	  subscribe block's recorded counterparty — a snapshot — while a producing
53	  system's consumers come from a live registry read, and change when the
54	  registry does. `message show` names both ends; the flow view draws the
55	  registry-derived side dashed.
56	
57	# Examples

59	<!-- Show: message list output, one subscribe block in a scaffold record,
60	one publishes block, and the resulting messagegroup in the topology. -->

9	// the same entry points and serves what they print. A second implementation
10	// would have to get the refusals right again: an unconfigured registry, an
11	// ambiguous reference, a message whose group carries no definition.

54		// the message's group: the applications on each end, and the channel

options.label: JSON Schema + Avro + Protobuf

options.label: Go emitter in the CLI

options.label: Shell out to a .NET tool
options.description: Wrap NJsonSchema/NSwag or quicktype as a dotnet tool the CLI invokes. Less code to own, mature type mapping — but adds a runtime prerequisite and output we don't control stylistically.

options.label: Emit into the template library
options.description: CLI passes the parsed field model as template values; the .cs.tmpl in intropy-templates renders it. Keeps all C# shape in the template repo, but couples generation to a template release.

questions.question: Which side of the wiring needs generated types?

options.label: Both subscribe and publishes
options.description: A consumer generates from the message it subscribes to; a producer generates from the schema its published message pins. Same code path, direction only picks which block supplies the pin.

options.label: Subscribe only for now
options.description: Consumers get the generated type; producers keep hand-authoring the contract record (the registry has no producer-authored schema flow yet).

Before I reformulate — what would you like to clarify?

For context on where the two finished explorers landed, in case it shapes your answer:

**What exists today.** The registry side records only *references*: `subscribe`/`publishes` blocks carry `dataschema` (logical xid) and `dataschemaurl` (immutable version pin, `internal/template/wiring.go:104-151`). `xregistry.Client` only ever calls `GET /export` (`internal/xregistry/client.go:143`) — fetching a schema *document* is net-new, and `MessageVersion.DataSchemaFormat` / `Schema.Format` are decoded but read nowhere.

**Where the C# type physically lives.** Not in this repo. `Contracts/` is a *sibling project* rendered from the `shared-contracts` template as a `spec.dependencies` edge (`internal/template/dependencies.go:117`), and its record body is hardcoded sample fields — an Order with four properties. So "generating the contract" means producing a field list that reaches a `.cs.tmpl` that currently has none.

**Two frictions with build-time generation specifically:**
1. It moves the work into intropy-framework/intropy-templates, not this repo — the CLI's part would shrink to "record the pin", which it already does. Almost nothing to implement here.
2. It cuts against a stated invariant: `sys create`/`sys update` never contact the registry, and external subscriptions "carry their own snapshot" (`catalog/concepts/messages-and-subscriptions.md:39-41`). A build that fetches from the registry needs registry access in CI and breaks offline builds — unless the fetched schema is cached/committed, at which point it's closer to the scaffold-time option.

There's a middle path the four options didn't offer: the CLI fetches the schema once at resolve time and **commits the schema document** into the project (alongside the pin), then generation from that local file happens at build time with no network. Offline builds, no drift, and re-pinning is an explicit CLI action.

One explorer is still mapping the templates/framework/registry repos — I'll fold that in before re-asking.

### shared-contracts — the whole template is 4 emitted files

`/Users/robinhultman/dev/intropy/integrio-intropy/intropy-templates/shared-contracts/skeleton/`
- `{{ .contract }}.cs.tmpl` → e.g. `ProductExported.cs` / `Order.cs`
- `OrderLine.cs.tmpl` → `OrderLine.cs` (hardcoded name, not parameterized)
- `{{ .name }}.csproj` (plain file, not `.tmpl`) → `Contracts.csproj`
- `AGENTS.md.tmpl`, `README.md.tmpl`, `.gitignore`

There is **no folder** — the record file sits at the project root. `Contracts/ProductExported.cs` is the path *within the system directory*: the project dir is named `Contracts`, so the file is `<system>/Contracts/ProductExported.cs`.

Parameter block, `/…/intropy-templates/shared-contracts/template.yaml:15-36`:

```yaml
spec:
  parameters:
    type: object
    required:
      - name
    properties:
      name:            # PascalCase project/namespace/assembly; conventionally "Contracts"
        pattern: "^[A-Z][A-Za-z0-9]*(\\.[A-Z][A-Za-z0-9]*)*$"
      contract:        # PascalCase name of the canonical record
        pattern: "^[A-Z][A-Za-z0-9]*$"
        default: Order
      empty:           # strip the sample fields, keep an empty shell
        type: boolean
        default: false
```

**There is no field/property list anywhere in the template data.** The record's shape is hardcoded sample text. `/…/shared-contracts/skeleton/{{ .contract }}.cs.tmpl:1-16`:

```gotemplate
namespace {{ .name }};
{{- if .empty }}

public record {{ .contract }}();
{{- else }}

// The canonical order contract: the extractor publishes exactly this shape …
public record {{ .contract }}(
    string OrderId,
    string CustomerId,
    DateTimeOffset OrderDate,
    IReadOnlyList<OrderLine> Lines);
{{- end }}
```

`/…/shared-contracts/skeleton/OrderLine.cs.tmpl:1-8` is the same idea (`Sku`, `Quantity`, `UnitPrice`), gated entirely on `not .empty`. So today the only two outcomes are **the Order sample** or **`public record X();`** — an empty shell whose only job is to make the pipeline generics compile (`template.yaml:35`). That empty shell is exactly the hole a schema-driven generator would fill.

The csproj is fixed and dependency-free (`/…/shared-contracts/skeleton/{{ .name }}.csproj:1-9`): `net10.0`, `Nullable`, `ImplicitUsings`. No `PackageReference` at all — nothing to hang a generator/analyzer off of yet.

### How it gets scaffolded (once per system)

Component templates declare it as a dependency rather than the user rendering it. `/…/intropy-templates/extractor/template.yaml:131-137` (loader is identical at `:113-119`):

```yaml
  dependencies:
    - template: shared-contracts
      output: '{{ .contracts }}'
      values:
        name: '{{ .contracts }}'
        contract: '{{ .contract }}'
        empty: '{{ .empty }}'
```

with `contracts: 'Contracts'` hardcoded as a derived value at `extractor/template.yaml:89`. `system-host` has the same dependency, conditional, at `/…/system-host/template.yaml:85-90` — and note it seeds the contract from the *first topic*: `contract: '{{ (index .topics 0).contract }}'`.

Dependencies render as a **sibling of the component output dir** and are skipped if already scaffolded — `/Users/robinhultman/dev/intropy/integrio-intropy/intropy-cli/internal/template/dependencies.go:56` (`parentDir := filepath.Dir(absOut)`), `:78` (`depDir := filepath.Join(parentDir, name)`), `:94-102` (existing `.intropy/scaffold.json` → `action: exists`, skipped). `--force` deliberately does not propagate (`:131-134`).

## 2. How a component's pipeline references the contract

**Shared project, not per-component.** The contract type is a `ProjectReference`, and there is a second, *local* per-component model beside it.

`/…/intropy-templates/extractor/skeleton/src/{{ .name }}.csproj.tmpl:26-30`:

```xml
  <ItemGroup>
    <!-- The shared contracts sibling is scaffolded by this template's
         spec.dependencies entry, so it exists whenever this project does. -->
    <ProjectReference Include="../../{{ .contracts }}/{{ .contracts }}.csproj" />
```

## Yes — a committed schema document, but I'd shape it differently than `.xreg.json`

Concretely, on a `--subscribe io.intropy.maxbo.product.export` against the seeded registry:

```

  ExportEvent.cs                 generated record (+ nested $defs records)
  schemas/

  .intropy/
    scaffold.json                already written by the dependency render
```

Two pieces of advice on the shape:

**Keep the schema document a plain `.json`.** It *is* a JSON Schema — served as `application/schema+json` with a `$schema` and `$id` — so a `.json` extension gets you editor validation, `$ref` navigation, and a reviewable PR diff. A bespoke `.xreg.json` extension buys nothing and costs tooling support. Store it byte-for-byte as served; that's what makes regeneration reproducible and drift detectable.

**The `.xreg.json` instinct is right about the *index*, though.** Something has to say "this schema file, at this pinned version, produced this type." The pin already exists in each component's `.intropy/scaffold.json` subscribe/publishes block — but that's the *sibling component's* record, and the Contracts project is the thing that gets built. So a realistic source generator reads a committed local document — which is the CLI-writes-the-document path regardless.

At that point the ledger is: build-time costs a new NuGet-packaged Roslyn generator in a repo with **zero** generation infrastructure to extend (no `.targets`, no `Target`/`Exec`, no schema library in `Directory.Packages.props`, and a contracts csproj with no `PackageReference` at all to hang an analyzer off), plus a version pin to keep in step with the CLI, plus generated code that no longer appears in the repo — a developer can't open `ExportEvent.cs`, `grep` for a property, or read the diff when a schema is re-pinned. In exchange it buys "the .cs cannot be hand-edited," which a `check` that regenerates and compares against the recorded digest also buys, in the CLI you already have.

The one MSBuild argument I'd take seriously is if you expect contract types to be *large and numerous* enough that committing them is noise. Nothing in the seed registry suggests that — two schemas, one nested `$def` each.

So: CLI generates at resolve time, both the document and the `.cs` get committed, and drift is a verification step rather than an architecture. If a source generator later earns its place, the committed documents are exactly the input it would need — this path doesn't foreclose it.

What do you recommend here?

Here's what I'd do, and why.

**Emitter — the CLI writes the `.cs`.** I argued the other way earlier from consistency ("intropy-templates owns all C# text"), but there's a fact that decides it: the Contracts project is rendered as a *dependency*, and `internal/template/dependencies.go:94-102` skips a dependency whose directory already has a scaffold record. So the template path renders the project exactly once — the second component in a system, subscribing to a second message, would never get a generated type. Generation has to add one file to an existing project, which is not what a skeleton render does. The principled line is that templates own *authored starting points* and a generator owns *derived artifacts*; `empty: true` already renders `public record X();` as a placeholder shell, and replacing that shell with the real record is the progression it was cut for.

**Artifacts — document, type, and index.** As laid out: verbatim `schemas/<id>.v<n>.json`, the generated record(s), and `.intropy/messages.json`. Without the document there's nothing local to regenerate from; without the index the project can't describe itself without walking sibling component directories.

**Drift — later, and not the check I first proposed.** Verifying the generated `.cs` against a digest fights a legitimate need: developers will add attributes and members to a contract type. The valuable signal isn't "the code changed", it's "the registry has moved past your pin" — which is a re-pin advisory, not a build gate, and `message show` is its natural home since it already reads the registry and knows the recorded version. So: record the version and digest now so the advisory is additive, and don't ship a gate in the first cut.

Two consequences worth flagging: property names get an explicit `[JsonPropertyName]` rather than relying on a serializer policy (the registry's own seed notes `GTIN` → `gTIN`, which no casing convention round-trips reliably), and an unsupported schema format warns and leaves the placeholder rather than failing the scaffold.

Writing this up now.

# Generate the .NET contract from an xRegistry message schema

## Context

The xregistry work on `feat/xregistry-message-integration` resolves a message
reference into full wiring — channel, CloudEvents type, and a schema pin —
and records it in the scaffold record's `subscribe`/`publishes` block. Every
value the registry owns now arrives without being typed by hand, except one:
the payload shape. `contract` is still a hand-typed PascalCase parameter, and
the record it names is a hardcoded four-field Order sample in
`intropy-templates/shared-contracts/skeleton/{{ .contract }}.cs.tmpl`, or —
with `empty: true` — an empty shell whose only job is to make the pipeline
generics compile.

So a developer subscribes to `io.intropy.maxbo.product.export`, gets the right
topic, pubsub, CloudEvents type and an immutable `dataschemaurl`, and then
transcribes twenty properties out of the registry's JSON Schema by hand into
a record that nothing checks. That transcription is the last manual step in
the flow, and it is the one most likely to be wrong.

The prior plans deliberately deferred this ("No codegen of types from
`dataschema` — an external tool's job", plan 003 line 92; "A2. External
code-generation tool … Not built here", the subscribe brainstorm line 31).

# Generate the .NET contract from an xRegistry message schema

## Context

The xregistry work on `feat/xregistry-message-integration` resolves a message
reference into full wiring — channel, CloudEvents type, and a schema pin — and
records it in the scaffold record's `subscribe`/`publishes` block. Every value
the registry owns now arrives without being typed by hand, except one: the
payload shape. `contract` is still a hand-typed PascalCase parameter, and the
record it names is a hardcoded four-field Order sample in
`intropy-templates/shared-contracts/skeleton/{{ .contract }}.cs.tmpl`, or —
with `empty: true` — an empty shell whose only job is to make the pipeline
generics compile.

So a developer subscribes to `io.intropy.maxbo.product.export`, gets the right
topic, pubsub, CloudEvents type and an immutable `dataschemaurl`, and then
transcribes the properties out of the registry's JSON Schema by hand into a
record that nothing checks. That transcription is the last manual step in the
flow and the one most likely to be wrong.

The prior plans deferred this ("No codegen of types from `dataschema` — an
external tool's job", plan 003 line 92). This plan reverses that non-goal, on
two findings those plans did not have:

- The registry serves exactly one schema format —
  `JsonSchema/draft/2020-12`, a single-value enum in
  `intropy-registry/src/registry/model.ts:26-35`. There is no format matrix.
- `GET /export` already inlines every schema **document**
  (`intropy-registry/src/registry/query.ts:5-6`). The CLI already fetches it
  on every resolve and discards the bodies, because
  `internal/xregistry/types.go:93-97` has no field for them. The input is in
  hand at zero extra HTTP cost.

**Outcome:** `intropy int create loader --subscribe <ref>` produces a Contracts
project containing the real record type for that message, and a second
component subscribing to a second message adds its type to the same project.

---

## Decisions

**The template emits every byte of C#; the CLI never does.** A customer forks
the template library, never the CLI — so anything a customer might want to
change must live in a template. That includes the JSON-Schema-to-C# *type
mapping*: a customer who wants `DateTime` instead of `DateTimeOffset`, or
`double` instead of `decimal`, must not have to fork Go code. The CLI
therefore hands the template a **language-neutral model in JSON Schema
vocabulary** (`type`, `format`, `required`, `$ref`) and the template decides
what each maps to, how nullability is spelled, whether properties carry
`[JsonPropertyName]`, and how identifiers are escaped.

**Structured data reaches the template through a reserved key.** This is what
`internal/template/reserved.go` exists for — its own doc says
`spec.parameters` is scalar-only by design and "the caller injects the
structures after validation, and the skeleton ranges over them", with
`spec.files` conditions over the same data deciding which files render.

**A second message re-renders the project with `RenderUpdate`.** The Contracts
project is a `spec.dependencies` sibling, and `dependencies.go:93-102` skips a
dependency whose directory already carries a scaffold record — so the create
path renders it exactly once per system. `template.RenderUpdate`
(`internal/template/render.go:129`) is the existing answer: it re-renders into
a directory that already holds a project, classifying each file as created,
unchanged, updated, or conflict against a baseline render, and refusing to
write past a conflict without `Force`. `sys update` already uses it for
exactly this shape of problem — adding a topic to a rendered host project
(`internal/system/update.go:175`). A hand-edited `Contracts.csproj` therefore
conflicts and is reported, rather than being silently clobbered.

**No drift gate, no digest, no verify.** The registry holds released messages;
updates are versioned and moving to a new version is a deliberate act. The pin
is recorded for provenance and that is all it is for.

### Who knows what

| Knowledge | Lives in |
| --- | --- |
| Fetching and pinning a schema | CLI (`internal/xregistry`) |
| Parsing JSON Schema 2020-12 into records and properties | CLI (`internal/contract`) |
| Identifier suggestion and collision detection | CLI (suggestion only) |
| `string`+`date-time` → which .NET type | **template** |
| Nullability syntax, `sealed record` vs `record`, XML docs | **template** |
| `[JsonPropertyName]`, C# keyword escaping | **template** |
| One file per message vs one file for all | **template** (`spec.files` + path templating) |

---

## What gets written

For `--subscribe io.intropy.maxbo.product.export` (schema `product-export.v1`,
default version 2, contract `ExportEvent`):

```
Contracts/
  Contracts.csproj                              template-owned
  ExportEvent.cs                                template-rendered from the model
  schemas/
    io.intropy.maxbo.product.export.v2.json     verbatim, as served
  .intropy/
    scaffold.json                               dependency render, unchanged
    messages.json                               new: the project's index
```

`messages.json` is the authoritative list of what this Contracts project
covers. It records references, never the parsed model — the model is derived
by re-parsing the committed documents, so there is one source of truth and a
re-render works offline:

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "messages": [
    {
      "message": "io.intropy.maxbo.product.export",
      "type": "io.intropy.maxbo.product.export",
      "contract": "ExportEvent",
      "dataschema": "/schemagroups/io.intropy.maxbo.product/schemas/product-export.v1",
      "dataschemaurl": "https://registry.intropy.io/schemagroups/io.intropy.maxbo.product/schemas/product-export.v1/versions/2",
      "schemaFile": "schemas/io.intropy.maxbo.product.export.v2.json"
    }
  ]
}
```

The committed schema document is the render input, not a drift tripwire: it is
what lets a customer who has forked the template library re-render their
contracts against a changed record style without contacting the registry.

---

## The reserved key

`ReservedMessagesKey = "messages"` in `internal/template/reserved.go`, injected
into **every** shared-contracts render — an empty list when there is no schema,
because `render.go` renders with `Option("missingkey=error")` and a template
referencing an absent key fails the render. The same word already means the
same thing in the system-host payload (`internal/system/payload.go:45-72`).

Shape handed to the template — JSON Schema vocabulary throughout:

```
messages:
  - message, type, contract, dataschema, dataschemaurl
    records:
      - name, doc
        properties:
          - name        PascalCased suggestion, collision-checked
            jsonName    verbatim from the schema
            schemaType  "string" | "integer" | "number" | "boolean" | "object" | "array"
            format      "date-time" | "uuid" | "int64" | ""
            required    bool
            array       bool
            ref         name of the $defs record, when the value is one
            enum        []string, when the schema constrains it
            doc         the schema's description
```

`name` is a suggestion the CLI collision-checks; the template owns the final
identifier, including keyword escaping. What the template does with it, e.g.:

```gotemplate
{{- define "csType" -}}
  {{- $t := "" -}}
  {{- if .ref }}{{ $t = .ref }}
  {{- else if eq .schemaType "string" -}}
    {{- if eq .format "date-time" }}{{ $t = "DateTimeOffset" }}
    {{- else if eq .format "uuid" }}{{ $t = "Guid" }}
    {{- else }}{{ $t = "string" }}{{ end -}}
  {{- else if eq .schemaType "integer" -}}
    {{- if eq .format "int64" }}{{ $t = "long" }}{{ else }}{{ $t = "int" }}{{ end -}}
  {{- else if eq .schemaType "number" }}{{ $t = "decimal" }}
  {{- else if eq .schemaType "boolean" }}{{ $t = "bool" }}{{ end -}}
  {{- if .array }}{{ $t = printf "IReadOnlyList<%s>" $t }}{{ end -}}
  {{- $t }}{{ if not .required }}?{{ end -}}
{{- end -}}
```

Every decision in that block is a customer's to change by forking the library.

---

## Implementation

### CLI — `intropy-cli`

**U1. Carry the schema document out of the export.**
`internal/xregistry/types.go` — add `Schema json.RawMessage \`json:"schema,omitempty"\``
to `Version` (line 93) and extend the doc comment at `types.go:8-13` to say
documents are inlined for schemas, so no second fetch is ever needed. Add
`DefaultSchemaVersion(doc, xid) (*Version, *Schema, error)` beside
`DefaultSchemaVersionXID` (line 228), returning version and parent resource so
callers get `Format`, `VersionID`, and `Schema` together; keep the existing
function delegating so `internal/message/registry.go:56,93` is untouched.
`ResolvedMessage` (line 22) gains `SchemaFormat`, `SchemaVersionID`,
`SchemaDocument json.RawMessage` — in-memory only; the blocks stay
reference-only. Fallback for a registry that does not inline:
`Client.SchemaDocument(ctx, absURL) ([]byte, error)`, read as bytes
(`application/schema+json`), used only when `Version.Schema` is empty.

**U2. Parse the schema into the neutral model.** New package
`internal/contract`: `Parse(doc []byte, opts) (*Model, error)`, knowing nothing
about templates, C#, or the filesystem. `santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/v5` is
already a direct dependency (`internal/template/values.go:13`) but is a
validator without a usefully traversable tree — use it to reject a document
that is not a valid schema, and decode into a purpose-built struct for
traversal. Rules: `$defs` entries become records; a `$ref` outside `#/$defs/`
is an error naming the ref, since remote refs are schemas the pin does not
cover; `additionalProperties` is ignored; identifier suggestion is PascalCase
with non-identifier characters stripped and a leading digit prefixed, and two

# Generate the .NET contract from an xRegistry message schema

## Context

The xregistry work on `feat/xregistry-message-integration` resolves a message
reference into full wiring — channel, CloudEvents type, and a schema pin — and
records it in the scaffold record's `subscribe`/`publishes` block. Every value
the registry owns now arrives without being typed by hand, except one: the
payload shape. `contract` is still a hand-typed PascalCase parameter, and the
record it names is a hardcoded four-field Order sample in
`intropy-templates/shared-contracts/skeleton/{{ .contract }}.cs.tmpl`, or —
with `empty: true` — an empty shell whose only job is to make the pipeline
generics compile.

So a developer subscribes to `io.intropy.maxbo.product.export`, gets the right
topic, pubsub, CloudEvents type and an immutable `dataschemaurl`, and then
transcribes the properties out of the registry's JSON Schema by hand into a
record that nothing checks. That transcription is the last manual step in the
flow and the one most likely to be wrong.

The prior plans deferred this ("No codegen of types from `dataschema` — an
external tool's job", plan 003 line 92). This plan reverses that non-goal, on
two findings those plans did not have:

- The registry serves exactly one schema format —
  `JsonSchema/draft/2020-12`, a single-value enum in
  `intropy-registry/src/registry/model.ts:26-35`. There is no format matrix.
- `GET /export` already inlines every schema **document**
  (`intropy-registry/src/registry/query.ts:5-6`). The CLI already fetches it
  on every resolve and discards the bodies, because
  `internal/xregistry/types.go:93-97` has no field for them. The input is in
  hand at zero extra HTTP cost.

**Outcome:** `intropy int create loader --subscribe <ref>` produces a Contracts
project containing the real record type for that message, and a second
component subscribing to a second message adds its type to the same project.

---

## Decisions

**The template emits every byte of C#; the CLI never does.** A customer forks
the template library, never the CLI — so anything a customer might want to
change must live in a template. That includes the JSON-Schema-to-C# *type
mapping*: a customer who wants `DateTime` instead of `DateTimeOffset`, or
`double` instead of `decimal`, must not have to fork Go code. The CLI
therefore hands the template a **language-neutral model in JSON Schema
vocabulary** (`type`, `format`, `required`, `$ref`) and the template decides
what each maps to, how nullability is spelled, whether properties carry
`[JsonPropertyName]`, and how identifiers are escaped.

**Structured data reaches the template through a reserved key.** This is what
`internal/template/reserved.go` exists for — its own doc says
`spec.parameters` is scalar-only by design and "the caller injects the
structures after validation, and the skeleton ranges over them", with
`spec.files` conditions over the same data deciding which files render.

**A second message re-renders the project with `RenderUpdate`.** The Contracts
project is a `spec.dependencies` sibling, and `dependencies.go:93-102` skips a
dependency whose directory already carries a scaffold record — so the create
path renders it exactly once per system. `template.RenderUpdate`
(`internal/template/render.go:129`) is the existing answer: it re-renders into
a directory that already holds a project, classifying each file as created,
unchanged, updated, or conflict against a baseline render, and refusing to
write past a conflict without `Force`. `sys update` already uses it for
exactly this shape of problem — adding a topic to a rendered host project
(`internal/system/update.go:175`). A hand-edited `Contracts.csproj` therefore
conflicts and is reported, rather than being silently clobbered.

**No drift gate, no digest, no verify.** The registry holds released messages;
updates are versioned and moving to a new version is a deliberate act. The pin
is recorded for provenance and that is all it is for.

### Who knows what

| Knowledge | Lives in |
| --- | --- |
| Fetching and pinning a schema | CLI (`internal/xregistry`) |
| Parsing JSON Schema 2020-12 into records and properties | CLI (`internal/contract`) |
| Identifier suggestion and collision detection | CLI (suggestion only) |
| `string`+`date-time` → which .NET type | **template** |
| Nullability syntax, `sealed record` vs `record`, XML docs | **template** |
| `[JsonPropertyName]`, C# keyword escaping | **template** |
| One file per message vs one file for all | **template** (`spec.files` + path templating) |

For `--subscribe io.intropy.maxbo.product.export` (schema `product-export.v1`,
default version 2, contract `ExportEvent`):

```
Contracts/
  Contracts.csproj                              template-owned
  ExportEvent.cs                                template-rendered from the model
  schemas/
    io.intropy.maxbo.product.export.v2.json     verbatim, as served
  .intropy/
    scaffold.json                               dependency render, unchanged
    messages.json                               new: the project's index
```

`messages.json` is the authoritative list of what this Contracts project
covers. It records references, never the parsed model — the model is derived
by re-parsing the committed documents, so there is one source of truth and a
re-render works offline:

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "messages": [
    {
      "message": "io.intropy.maxbo.product.export",
      "type": "io.intropy.maxbo.product.export",
      "contract": "ExportEvent",
      "dataschema": "/schemagroups/io.intropy.maxbo.product/schemas/product-export.v1",
      "dataschemaurl": "https://registry.intropy.io/schemagroups/io.intropy.maxbo.product/schemas/product-export.v1/versions/2",
      "schemaFile": "schemas/io.intropy.maxbo.product.export.v2.json"
    }
  ]
}
```

The committed schema document is the render input, not a drift tripwire: it is

`ReservedMessagesKey = "messages"` in `internal/template/reserved.go`, injected

```
            format      "date-time" | "uuid" | "int64" | ""
            required    bool

            ref         name of the $defs record, when the value is one

            doc         the schema's description
```

`name` is a suggestion the CLI collision-checks; the template owns the final

```gotemplate
  {{- else if eq .schemaType "string" -}}

  {{- else if eq .schemaType "integer" -}}
    {{- if eq .format "int64" }}{{ $t = "long" }}{{ else }}{{ $t = "int" }}{{ end -}}
  {{- else if eq .schemaType "number" }}{{ $t = "decimal" }}
  {{- else if eq .schemaType "boolean" }}{{ $t = "bool" }}{{ end -}}
  {{- if .array }}{{ $t = printf "IReadOnlyList<%s>" $t }}{{ end -}}
  {{- $t }}{{ if not .required }}?{{ end -}}
```

- `GET /export` already inlines every schema **document**
  (`intropy-registry/src/registry/query.ts:5-6`). The CLI already fetches it
  on every resolve and discards the bodies, because
  `internal/xregistry/types.go:93-97` has no field for them. The input is in
  hand at zero extra HTTP cost.

**Outcome:** `intropy int create loader --subscribe <ref>` produces a Contracts
project containing the real record type for that message, and a second
component subscribing to a second message adds its type to the same project.

---

## Decisions

**The template emits every byte of C#; the CLI never does.** A customer forks
the template library, never the CLI — so anything a customer might want to
change must live in a template. That includes the JSON-Schema-to-C# *type
mapping*: a customer who wants `DateTime` instead of `DateTimeOffset`, or
`double` instead of `decimal`, must not have to fork Go code. The CLI
therefore hands the template a **language-neutral model in JSON Schema
vocabulary** (`type`, `format`, `required`, `$ref`) and the template decides
what each maps to, how nullability is spelled, whether properties carry
`[JsonPropertyName]`, and how identifiers are escaped.

**Structured data reaches the template through a reserved key.** This is what
`internal/template/reserved.go` exists for — its own doc says
`spec.parameters` is scalar-only by design and "the caller injects the
structures after validation, and the skeleton ranges over them", with
`spec.files` conditions over the same data deciding which files render.

**A second message re-renders the project with `RenderUpdate`.** The Contracts
project is a `spec.dependencies` sibling, and `dependencies.go:93-102` skips a
dependency whose directory already carries a scaffold record — so the create
path renders it exactly once per system. `template.RenderUpdate`
(`internal/template/render.go:129`) is the existing answer: it re-renders into
a directory that already holds a project, classifying each file as created,
unchanged, updated, or conflict against a baseline render, and refusing to
write past a conflict without `Force`. `sys update` already uses it for
exactly this shape of problem — adding a topic to a rendered host project
(`internal/system/update.go:175`). A hand-edited `Contracts.csproj` therefore
conflicts and is reported, rather than being silently clobbered.

**No drift gate, no digest, no verify.** The registry holds released messages;
updates are versioned and moving to a new version is a deliberate act. The pin
is recorded for provenance and that is all it is for.

### Who knows what

| Knowledge | Lives in |
| --- | --- |
| Fetching and pinning a schema | CLI (`internal/xregistry`) |
| Parsing JSON Schema 2020-12 into records and properties | CLI (`internal/contract`) |
| Identifier suggestion and collision detection | CLI (suggestion only) |
| `string`+`date-time` → which .NET type | **template** |
| Nullability syntax, `sealed record` vs `record`, XML docs | **template** |
| `[JsonPropertyName]`, C# keyword escaping | **template** |
| One file per message vs one file for all | **template** (`spec.files` + path templating) |

---

## What gets written

For `--subscribe io.intropy.maxbo.product.export` (schema `product-export.v1`,
default version 2, contract `ExportEvent`):

```
Contracts/
  Contracts.csproj                              template-owned
  ExportEvent.cs                                template-rendered from the model
  schemas/
    io.intropy.maxbo.product.export.v2.json     verbatim, as served
  .intropy/
    scaffold.json                               dependency render, unchanged
    messages.json                               new: the project's index
```

`messages.json` is the authoritative list of what this Contracts project
covers. It records references, never the parsed model — the model is derived
by re-parsing the committed documents, so there is one source of truth and a
re-render works offline:

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "messages": [
    {
      "message": "io.intropy.maxbo.product.export",
      "type": "io.intropy.maxbo.product.export",
      "contract": "ExportEvent",
      "dataschema": "/schemagroups/io.intropy.maxbo.product/schemas/product-export.v1",
      "dataschemaurl": "https://registry.intropy.io/schemagroups/io.intropy.maxbo.product/schemas/product-export.v1/versions/2",
      "schemaFile": "schemas/io.intropy.maxbo.product.export.v2.json"
    }
  ]
}
```

The committed schema document is the render input, not a drift tripwire: it is
what lets a customer who has forked the template library re-render their
contracts against a changed record style without contacting the registry.

---

## The reserved key

`ReservedMessagesKey = "messages"` in `internal/template/reserved.go`, injected
into **every** shared-contracts render — an empty list when there is no schema,
because `render.go` renders with `Option("missingkey=error")` and a template
referencing an absent key fails the render. The same word already means the
same thing in the system-host payload (`internal/system/payload.go:45-72`).

Shape handed to the template — JSON Schema vocabulary throughout:

```
messages:
  - message, type, contract, dataschema, dataschemaurl
    records:
      - name, doc
        properties:
          - name        PascalCased suggestion, collision-checked
            jsonName    verbatim from the schema
            schemaType  "string" | "integer" | "number" | "boolean" | "object" | "array"
            format      "date-time" | "uuid" | "int64" | ""
            required    bool
            array       bool
            ref         name of the $defs record, when the value is one
            enum        []string, when the schema constrains it
            doc         the schema's description
```

`name` is a suggestion the CLI collision-checks; the template owns the final
identifier, including keyword escaping. What the template does with it, e.g.:

```gotemplate
{{- define "csType" -}}
  {{- $t := "" -}}
  {{- if .ref }}{{ $t = .ref }}
  {{- else if eq .schemaType "string" -}}
    {{- if eq .format "date-time" }}{{ $t = "DateTimeOffset" }}
    {{- else if eq .format "uuid" }}{{ $t = "Guid" }}
    {{- else }}{{ $t = "string" }}{{ end -}}
  {{- else if eq .schemaType "integer" -}}
    {{- if eq .format "int64" }}{{ $t = "long" }}{{ else }}{{ $t = "int" }}{{ end -}}
  {{- else if eq .schemaType "number" }}{{ $t = "decimal" }}
  {{- else if eq .schemaType "boolean" }}{{ $t = "bool" }}{{ end -}}
  {{- if .array }}{{ $t = printf "IReadOnlyList<%s>" $t }}{{ end -}}
  {{- $t }}{{ if not .required }}?{{ end -}}
{{- end -}}
```

Every decision in that block is a customer's to change by forking the library.

---

## Implementation

### CLI — `intropy-cli`

**U1. Carry the schema document out of the export.**
`internal/xregistry/types.go` — add `Schema json.RawMessage \`json:"schema,omitempty"\``
to `Version` (line 93) and extend the doc comment at `types.go:8-13` to say
documents are inlined for schemas, so no second fetch is ever needed. Add
`DefaultSchemaVersion(doc, xid) (*Version, *Schema, error)` beside
`DefaultSchemaVersionXID` (line 228), returning version and parent resource so
callers get `Format`, `VersionID`, and `Schema` together; keep the existing
function delegating so `internal/message/registry.go:56,93` is untouched.
`ResolvedMessage` (line 22) gains `SchemaFormat`, `SchemaVersionID`,
`SchemaDocument json.RawMessage` — in-memory only; the blocks stay
reference-only. Fallback for a registry that does not inline:
`Client.SchemaDocument(ctx, absURL) ([]byte, error)`, read as bytes
(`application/schema+json`), used only when `Version.Schema` is empty.

**U2. Parse the schema into the neutral model.** New package

validator without a usefully traversable tree — use it to reject a document
that is not a valid schema, and decode into a purpose-built struct for

is an error naming the ref, since remote refs are schemas the pin does not
cover; `additionalProperties` is ignored; identifier suggestion is PascalCase
with non-identifier characters stripped and a leading digit prefixed, and two

- A template's message **direction** is derived from its block kind: an
  extractor publishes, a loader subscribes, a transactional integration
  wires no messages. The flags follow it: `--publishes` for producing
  templates, `--subscribe` for consuming templates.
- **message** is a message definition: a registry entry (`message list`,
  `message show <ref>`) or a producing component's `publishes` declaration.
  A subscription is written to the record as a `subscribe` block; a
  producer's as `publishes`. **event** is prose for the runtime occurrence
  of a message, never a scaffold value. `contract` survives only where the
  .NET shared-project type name is literally meant — transitional.
- `->` for a transition (`1.0 -> 1.1`), ` @ ` for a pin (`api @ 1.2.0`).
  Never mix the two in one message.
- A commit SHA is shown short (7 chars) unless the full value is the point.

content.text:
CLI half is complete: 19 packages green, `go vet` clean, `gofmt` clean.

## What landed

**`internal/xregistry`** — `Version.Schema` picks up the JSON Schema body that `/export` was already sending and the client was discarding; `DefaultSchemaVersion` returns the resource and version together (format lives on one, document and xid on the other). `Client.SchemaDocument` is the fallback for a service that serves collections without documents. Notably, `Resolve` does *not* fetch it — I tried that first and it broke three existing tests by turning an ambiguous-producer error into a fetch error. Resolution answers "what wiring does this message need", and a service that omits documents answers that fine.

**`internal/contract`** (new) — parses 2020-12 into records and properties in JSON Schema vocabulary, plus the project index and the committed documents. No C# anywhere in it.

**`internal/template`** — `ReservedMessagesKey`, and `contracts.go` holding the whole seam: build the model before anything renders, inject for shared-library renders, `RenderUpdate` when the project already exists, commit the document and index after.

## Two things worth knowing

**Property names get no `[JsonPropertyName]` from me.** The plan had the CLI deciding that; it's C# knowledge, so it moved to the template along with the type mapping. The model exposes `jsonName` verbatim next to a PascalCased `name` suggestion, and the template decides what to do with both — including keyword escaping. The `gTIN` case is a test in the fixture library rather than a rule in Go.

**The underscore rule changed during implementation.** `order_id` → `OrderId`, not `Order_Id`. Dropping the underscore can make two schema names collide, but `uniqueIdentifiers` fails naming both properties, so the collision is caught rather than silently emitting a name nobody would write.

## Tests

12 unit tests in `internal/contract` (the two real registry seed documents copied verbatim as fixtures) and 6 end-to-end in `cmd/intropy/int_create_contract_test.go`. The one that protects the design is the second component subscribing to a second message — trace confirms `skipped` → `updated Contracts/Contracts.cs`, which is the case a template-render approach structurally could not serve. I also added a test for `--force` after writing the conflict error, since an untested remediation is worse than none.

Fixing the drift warning was not in the plan — the trace showed it firing on every second component, because `contract` legitimately differs per message once a project holds several.

## Not done

- **The `intropy-templates` half.** Until `shared-contracts` renders from `.messages`, this produces nothing against the real library — the CLI injects a key no skeleton reads. My fixture library contains a working `csType` mapping that can seed it. That's a different repo and plan 003 governs its `v0.10.0-rc.1` tag, so I've left the sequencing to you.
- **The `dotnet build` gate.** Can't exist until the above lands; generated C# that doesn't compile is the one failure mode nothing currently catches.
- `TestRealSystemHostDependencyWhen` fails, but it fails identically without my changes — a stale expectation against the template repo's current branch.

Want me to do the templates side?

I am having second thoughts. Would it be better to point another tool (that already exists) at the message file and have that generate the pocos? That would be something the developer did after scaffold

Yes, I think that's the better trade — and the main reason isn't the code volume, it's schema coverage.

My parser handles a deliberate subset: objects, arrays, local `$defs`/`$ref`, enums, string formats, nullable unions. That covers both of the registry's current seed schemas exactly. It does *not* handle `oneOf`, `allOf`, `anyOf`, `const`, tuple-typed arrays, `patternProperties`, or discriminators — and my code hard-fails on those by design. The first customer schema using `allOf` for composition turns a scaffold into an error, and then I'm growing a JSON Schema implementation in Go, which is a bad place to be. NJsonSchema has had years of that.

There's also a point in its favor that comes from your own fork principle: a tool config committed **in the Contracts project** is more forkable than the template library. The customer edits it in their own repo, no fork of anything required. That's strictly better than what I built, where changing `decimal` to `double` means forking intropy-templates.

## What survives, and what I'd delete

The important thing: **the enabling work isn't the parser.** Every version of this needs the CLI to get the schema document onto disk with its provenance, and that's what U1 and U3 do:

- **Keep** — `Version.Schema` picking the document out of `/export` (zero extra requests), `Client.SchemaDocument` as fallback, `schemaSource` on the resolutions, and `internal/contract`'s index and document commit: `Contracts/schemas/<message>.v<n>.json` plus `.intropy/messages.json`. That's the message file you'd point the tool at, and it's already tested.
- **Delete** — `parse.go`, `ident.go`, the `messages` reserved key, `template/contracts.go`, the `RenderUpdate` plumbing in `dependencies.go`, and the template-side mapping. Roughly 600 of the ~900 lines, and the `internal/contract` tests shrink to the index/document half.

That also unblocks shipping: without the reserved key, this branch no longer waits on a template release, so the plan-003 coupling disappears.

## Two things I'd want to get right

**The class name is a coupling point.** The pipeline references the type by the `contract` value — `DeserializeStep<ExportEvent, Context>`, `TopicRef<ExportEvent>`. So the tool has to be told to name the root class exactly that, and the generated namespace has to be `Contracts`. NSwag takes `/ClassName` and `/Namespace`; if the developer runs the tool with defaults they'll get something that doesn't match and won't compile. So the scaffold should emit the *exact* invocation, not a prose instruction — ideally a committed config file the tool reads, so the command is argument-free and reproducible.

**A skipped step fails silently, not loudly.** `empty: true` renders `public record ExportEvent();` — that compiles. A developer who never runs the tool gets a pipeline that deserializes every message into an empty record and drops the payload at runtime. Worth making the shell not compile, or having the generated README/AGENTS.md make the step impossible to miss.

My suggestion for the shape: the CLI commits the document and index; the **template** emits the tool config and the invocation into the Contracts project. That keeps "how types are generated" template-owned and customer-forkable, and the developer's step is one command with no arguments to get wrong.

Before I reshape it — which tool did you have in mind? If there's one already in use in the org, that decides the config format and the naming flags, and I'd rather build the scaffold around it than guess at NSwag's `jsonschema2csclient`.
No I havent selected a tool but I agree that we must. What would you recommend?

content.text:
I tested both against your actual seed schemas, compiled the output on net10.0, and round-tripped real payloads. There's a decisive finding.

## Recommendation: quicktype

**NSwag disqualifies itself on your current schema.** `jsonschema2csclient` with `/JsonLibrary:SystemTextJson` emits `[EnumMember(Value = "product-attribute")]` — a Newtonsoft/DataContract attribute that System.Text.Json ignores. So a perfectly valid payload from your own `product-export.v1` throws:

```
FAILED: JsonException: The JSON value could not be converted to Contracts.FilesEntityType
```

There is no flag to fix it — `jsonschema2csclient` has no enum options at all. The only escapes are switching the contracts project to Newtonsoft or hand-editing generated code. quicktype instead generates a real `JsonConverter` with both directions mapped, and round-trips correctly:

```
entityType=ProductAttribute
roundtrip={"container":"exports","exportId":"run-7","files":[{"blob":"a.jsonl","entityType":"product-attribute",...}]}
```

Note it also omits absent optionals rather than writing `"startedAt":null` — which matches the note in your own `schema.yaml` that nulls are omitted.

| | NSwag 14.7.1 | quicktype 23 |
|---|---|---|
| 2020-12 `$defs`/`$ref` | resolves | resolves |
| hyphenated enum, STJ | **throws** | correct both ways |
| `description` → XML docs | yes | yes |
| optional → nullable | with `/GenerateOptionalPropertiesAsNullable` | default |
| `format: uuid` → `Guid` | yes | yes |
| integer / collection | `int`, `IReadOnlyList<>` configurable | `long`, `T[]` fixed |
| shape | `partial record` + setters | `partial class` + setters |
| toolchain | dotnet tool, pinnable in `dotnet-tools.json` | Node, `npx quicktype@<version>` |

## Three honest caveats

**Neither tool names nested types reliably.** NSwag names them after the *property* (`files` → `Files`, `unitConversions` → `UnitConversions` — a record for one conversion, named plural). quicktype got `ExportEventFile` right from the `$defs` key on one schema and then produced `Updated` for `$defs/UnitConversion` on the other. I don't have an explanation for that second one. It's cosmetic rather than blocking, because the templates only ever reference the *root* type — `DeserializeStep<ExportEvent, Context>`, `TopicRef<ExportEvent>` — and `--top-level` controls that precisely. Nested names stay inside the contracts project.

**The pipeline templates must change.** quicktype wires its converters through `Converter.Settings`, not property attributes, so today's `JsonSerializer.Deserialize<T>(json, new JsonSerializerOptions { PropertyNameCaseInsensitive = true })` in the loader's Deserializer fails exactly like NSwag did. Using the generated `ExportEvent.FromJson(json)` / `ToJson()` works. That's a small template edit, and arguably a better seam anyway — serialization policy owned by the contracts project instead of re-specified inline in every step.

**Node in a .NET shop.** That's the real cost. If it's unacceptable, the fallback is NSwag with Newtonsoft in the contracts project, which drags Newtonsoft into the pipeline too — I'd rather have the Node dependency. (Untested third option: Corvus.JsonSchema has the best 2020-12 fidelity in .NET and handles `oneOf`/`allOf`, but generates `JsonElement`-backed structs, not POCOs — a different programming model entirely, not a drop-in.)

## What it means for the code

`internal/contract`'s parser and the `messages` reserved key come out, as discussed. The document-and-index half stays and becomes the tool's input:

```
npx quicktype@23 --src-lang schema --lang csharp --framework SystemTextJson \
  --namespace Contracts --top-level ExportEvent \
  -o ExportEvent.cs schemas/io.intropy.maxbo.product.export.v2.json
```

Every argument in that line is already in `messages.json` — `contract` is `--top-level`, `schemaFile` is the input, the output name follows the contract. So the template can emit a script that reads the index and regenerates everything, argument-free.

# xRegistry Code Generation CLI

[![Python Test](https://github.com/xregistry/codegen/actions/workflows/test.yml/badge.svg?branch=main)](https://github.com/xregistry/codegen/actions/workflows/test.yml)

Generate production-ready, type-safe messaging SDKs from [xRegistry](https://xregistry.io/) message catalog definitions. One command gives you compile-ready producer/consumer code with tests, dependency management, and protocol-specific bindings.

## Quick Start

**1. Install** (Docker or pip):

```bash
# Docker (recommended - no Python needed)
docker pull ghcr.io/xregistry/codegen/xrcg:latest

# Or via pip
pip install git+https://github.com/xregistry/codegen.git
```

**2. Generate a Kafka producer** from a sample definition:

```bash
# Using Docker (Linux/macOS)
docker run --rm -v $(pwd):/work ghcr.io/xregistry/codegen/xrcg:latest \
  generate --projectname PrinterEvents --language py --style kafkaproducer \
  --definitions https://raw.githubusercontent.com/xregistry/codegen/main/samples/message-definitions/inkjet.xreg.json \
  --output ./generated
```


```bash
  --definitions https://raw.githubusercontent.com/xregistry/codegen/main/samples/message-definitions/inkjet.xreg.json \
  --output ./generated
```

content.text:
Tested it. **No — not worth adopting for Intropy**, on two independent grounds.

## It generates the layer you already own

The C# styles are all transport SDKs: `amqpproducer/consumer`, `ehproducer/consumer`, `egproducer`, `sbproducer/consumer`, `kafkaproducer/consumer`, `mqttclient`, plus Azure Functions variants. **No Dapr style**, and no plain data style for C# beyond an internal `_schemas/data` template. What it produces — producer/consumer classes, envelope handling, csproj, Testcontainers tests — is exactly what Intropy.Framework and the pipeline steps already provide. Adopting it means running a second, competing messaging stack, or fighting the tool to emit only the data classes.

To be clear about method: I didn't execute `xrcg` itself (pip-from-git or Docker), I read its C# template set — which settles the altitude question — and then tested the engine it delegates data classes to.

## Its data path degrades your schemas

Data classes come from **Avrotize**, and the default JSON Schema → Avro → C# route on your real `product-export.v1` produced:

- root type named `Document` (the `title` ignored)
- namespace `Contracts.Io.Intropy.Registry.Io.Schemagroups` — derived from `$id`, with `Io` twice
- `format: date-time` → **`long?`**
- enum symbols mangled to `product_attribute` (Avro forbids hyphens)
- the optional enum turned into an `EntityTypeUnion` wrapper class with a custom converter
- camelCase properties, plus generated test projects

That's the Avro hop, not tool sloppiness: Avro has no hyphens in enum symbols, no native date-time, and unions where JSON Schema has optionality.

Its newer **JSON Structure** route (`j2s` → `s2cs`) is genuinely close to ideal — flat `namespace Contracts`, PascalCase with `[JsonPropertyName]`, C# `required` modifiers, `DateTimeOffset?` preserved, `ExportEventFile` named from the `$defs` key, and an enum converter mapping `"product-attribute"` ↔ `ProductAttribute` both ways. But it drops `$ref` array items:

```csharp
public required List<object> Files { get; set; }
```

`j2s` does emit the ref (as `items.type.$ref`); `s2cs` doesn't follow it. And `--root-class-name ExportEvent` is ignored — still `Document`. Both defects persist together, so it's not usable today.

## So quicktype stands

Worth noting for later, though: **avrotize `s2cs` is the closest thing to ideal**, because it's attribute-based. No `Converter.Settings` dependency means the pipeline's existing `JsonSerializer.Deserialize<T>(json, options)` call would work unchanged — no template edit to the Deserializer step, which is quicktype's one real cost. If those two bugs were fixed it would beat quicktype outright. They're small and specific enough to be worth filing upstream.

The one idea worth borrowing from xregistry/codegen is that it reads the registry document directly rather than a bare schema file. But your CLI already does that resolution and records it — that job is done.

Caveat on all of this: two schemas, current tool versions, the flags I could find. Everything's reproducible in `scratchpad/spike/` if you want to poke at the generated output.

Shall I reshape the branch around quicktype — drop the parser and reserved key, keep the document-and-index half, and have the template emit the regeneration script?

content.text:
That settles it. Avrotize in isolation was exactly what I tested — and the gap isn't the wrapper, it's that **neither of its two paths handles your schemas completely**:

| | `j2a` → `a2cs` (Avro) | `j2s` → `s2cs` (JSON Structure) |
|---|---|---|
| composite types (`$ref`) | `List<ExportEventFile>` ✓ | `List<object>`, and a scalar ref **crashes**: `cannot use 'dict' as a dict key` |
| `format: date-time` | `long?` ✗ | `DateTimeOffset?` ✓ |
| hyphenated enum | mangled to `product_attribute`, wrapped in a union class ✗ | correct `"product-attribute"` ↔ `ProductAttribute` converter ✓ |
| namespace | `Contracts.Io.Intropy.Registry.Io.Schemagroups` ✗ | flat `Contracts` ✓ |
| root class name | `Document` ✗ | fixable — the intermediate's `name` drives it (though `--root-class-name` doesn't wire through) |

Each path has what the other lacks. The `s2cs` ref gap is decisive because **every** schema in your registry uses arrays of `$defs` objects — `files` in product-export, `unitConversions` and `imageGuids` in product-updated. And the crash happens on the very construct `j2s` itself emits (`{"type": {"$ref": ...}}`), just at property level rather than inside `items`, so it's not an exotic input.

So: quicktype remains the recommendation. It went JSON Schema → C# directly, with no lossy intermediate, and got refs, date-time, uuid, hyphenated enums, and optionality all correct on both of your real schemas.

What would flip it: `s2cs` learning to follow definition references. It's the better shape otherwise — attribute-based, so the pipeline's existing `JsonSerializer.Deserialize<T>(json, options)` call keeps working and no template edit to the Deserializer step is needed, which is quicktype's one real cost. Two small, specific, reproducible bugs; I can write them up as issues if you want to nudge it.

Ready to reshape the branch around quicktype: drop `parse.go`/`ident.go`/the `messages` reserved key/`template/contracts.go`, keep the document-and-index half that's already tested, and have the template emit the regeneration script driven by `messages.json`. Say go and I'll do it.
ok and it is not that i have defined my schemas in a bad way?

No — and I want to be specific rather than reassuring.

Your schemas use a small, conservative, idiomatic subset:

- `$defs` + `#/$defs/X` — the *standard* mechanism in 2020-12 (draft-07's `definitions` was renamed to exactly this)
- optionality by omission from `required` — the correct idiom, better than `"type": ["string", "null"]`
- `format: date-time` / `format: uuid` — standard registered formats
- `additionalProperties: false`, `title`, `description`, `$id`, `$schema` — all present and correct
- no `oneOf`, `allOf`, `anyOf`, `if`/`then`, `patternProperties`, tuple arrays, or recursive refs — none of the genuinely hard constructs

The strongest evidence: **my own hand-rolled 300-line Go parser handled both schemas completely on the first run**, and so did quicktype. Two independent implementations got them fully right. What failed were specific bugs in specific tools — NSwag pairing a Newtonsoft attribute with a System.Text.Json converter, and avrotize's `s2cs` not following definition references at all (crashing outright on a scalar one). Neither is a reaction to anything unusual in your schemas.

Two honest observations anyway:

**Hyphenated enum values are the single most tool-sensitive choice in there.** `product-attribute` is perfectly legal and common in JSON APIs, and I would *not* contort the wire format to suit a broken generator. But it's worth knowing that's the thing which separated the tools, so if you ever evaluate another one, that enum is the first test to run.

**`product-export.v1` at `versions/2` reads oddly.** A schema whose id says `v1` sitting at registry version 2 is mildly confusing — is `.v1` the major line, with registry versions as the minor? That's a naming decision, not a correctness one, and unrelated to codegen. Just flagging it since you asked broadly.

The forward-looking risk is the opposite of a schema problem: if a future message *does* need `oneOf` or `allOf` for polymorphism, tool choice gets much harder and my hand-rolled parser would hard-fail. quicktype at least handles unions pragmatically. That's another argument for not owning the parser.

Still happy to reshape around quicktype whenever you say go.
Ok then quicktype it is
Executing the reshape.
